encoding.title: Encoding and decoding
encoding.lead: Encoding packs pictures into a small file. Decoding unpacks them again. Only then can you show or edit them.

basics.heading: 1. There and back
basics.text: When encoding, many pictures become one file. When decoding, every picture is rebuilt from the file. Both sides need a shared recipe for that: the codec.

codecs.heading: Three well-known recipes

h264.name: H.264
h264.text: The classic. Almost every device can play it, including phones and school computers.

vp9.name: VP9
vp9.text: From Google, made for websites. At the same quality the file is often smaller than with H.264.

av1.name: AV1
av1.text: The new, open recipe. The files are very small, but encoding takes longer and older devices cannot always play it.

codecs.app: In Jelly Cut you choose the codec when you export: H.264, VP9 or AV1. Some players cannot open every codec.

edit.heading: 2. Cutting is not always the same
edit.text: A keyframe (K) is a complete picture. If you cut exactly at a keyframe, the parts can simply be copied. Nothing is recalculated and nothing is lost.
edit.text2: If you cut in between, the app first has to decode the pictures, make the cut and encode everything again. That is exactly where quality is lost.
edit.captionKey: Lossless: the parts are simply copied.
edit.captionMiddle: With loss: the pictures are encoded again.
edit.tip: In the fine cut of Jelly Cut you can see which pictures are keyframes. There you can jump exactly to a keyframe.

loss.heading: 3. A copy of a copy
loss.text: Every new encoding leaves something out. If you encode a picture again and again, you see the damage. Try it.
loss.note: Here we use JPEG as an example. Real video codecs lose detail in other ways, but the principle is the same.
loss.diffLabel: Difference from the original, amplified {amplify} times

app.heading: 4. What Jelly Cut does on export
app.text: In the editor you see the pictures as pictures, not as a file. Jelly Cut decodes them, draws texts, stickers and filters on them and encodes everything once more on export.
app.text2: That is why the export setting matters. It decides how small the file gets and how much quality stays.

settings.resolution: How many pixels the picture has. More is sharper but needs more space.
settings.fps: How many pictures per second. For school 30 is usually enough.
settings.quality: Good, Small or Very small. This sets the bitrate: the lower, the smaller and less exact.
settings.format: MP4 for videos. GIF for short loops without sound.
settings.codec: H.264 plays almost everywhere. VP9 and AV1 are often smaller.

tips.heading: 5. Tips
tips.once: Cut once and export once. Every round of export makes the picture worse.
tips.originals: Keep your original files. With them you can always export again, and better.
tips.final: For the finished video: quality Good. For a quick message, Small is enough.
tips.reexport: Do not export a finished file again to change it. Take the project instead.
tips.h264: If you want to be sure that every computer can open the file: MP4 with H.264.
